title: Why the Agent was the Biggest Villain in the 49ers' Brandon Aiyuk Debacle
text: So, I got one more thing I want to talk about, and it's Brandon Iayuk, but I think this is interesting. Bear with me on here. We've spent all off season talking about the IU debacle and who's at fault. Obviously, Brandon Aayuk bears a ton of responsibility for his actions. In my opinion, the Niners do as well. I don't think they're 100% innocent on this, but to me, the biggest villain in this whole story is the agent Ryan Williams. Okay, this guy was representing John Lynch and Brandon Aayuk at the same time. He had a conflict of interest. It's not all right. And you know, maybe this is Brandon Aayuk's fault, too, dude. He should have known. Maybe she should have fired him earlier. But like every player deserves an agent who has their best interest at heart. Did Ryan have Brandon's best interest at heart or did he have the 49ers best interest at heart? I submit I argue that he had the Ner's best interest at heart. Here's why I say that. If Aayuk had a good agent who wasn't also representing John Lynch, as soon as the guarantees were void, first of all, the agent would have protected him from the uh voided guarantees. But let's say that let's say Ryan Williams did try to call IU and say, "Look, man, you got to show up. You got to show up. They're going to void your guarantees." And I ignored him and didn't go. And they voided the guarantees. Dude, I don't give a damn what the agent felt or if he felt he was ignored. He a good agent who only has one person's interest at heart and doesn't have a conflict of interest releases that story in July of last year. Hey Adam Shfter, hey Tom Pelisero. Hey Mike Silver. Guess what the Niners just did to my client. It's outrageous. You should know. Let's make this a huge story. That's what any agent would do. What did Ryan Williams do? What'd he do? I don't know what he did. We didn't hear about this until November. How did keeping this a secret benefit Brandon? It didn't. And look, Brandon is 28, almost 29. He's not a child. It's his fault for hiring Ryan Williams and not understanding the inherent uh conflict of interest that there would be. But like, dude, Ryan, horrible, we all should have known about the void of guarantees in a year ago. That's your job. You got to fight for your guy. You got to fight for your guy. Instead, it see it seems like you helped keep this um under the rug. That doesn't help your guy. that helps the NerS. Yo, when John Lynch and Kyle Shanahan were asked about this weekly and they said that Brandon's close to coming back, you should have been the one to go to Adam Shfter and say, "What are they talking about? He's not close to coming back. They voided his guarantees. My client isn't going to play without guarantees. This is unprofessional. That's what he should have done, but he didn't." And that's why I feel like he's very much at fault. If the not if he if there had been a different agent, maybe Aayuk would have been able to be uh you know, maybe this would have been avoided. Maybe he'd be released by now. But a big reason we're at a standoff is because the person who was supposed to be Aayuk's advocate wasn't. He was during the contract negotiation, but not after that. Again, if he was, we would have heard about this in July, not November. And it seems to me, I don't know, we'd have to ask Mike Silver, but it seems to me like Mike Silver eventually reported this with Diana Rini on their own, not because Ryan Williams gave him the green light because they found out. I I I I almost wonder if Ryan Williams didn't want him to report it. I wonder how many people at the NFL Network knew about it and didn't say anything because that seems to be how people do business these days in sports media, right? You find things out that the team doesn't want you to know and instead of reporting it, you tell the team so they can tell you when or when to report it or or not to report it. And then you can create a business working relationship with them because they trust you even though now you've just compromised your journalistic integrity. Just saying we're learning how this industry works. It's a dirty game. and the people who don't get play ball get pushed out. But what I want to say is it feels like the people who have been playing ball have been getting outed and it's a bad look. And I don't think sports fans want their insiders in the pocket of the teams they cover. So shout out to the ones who aren't and the ones who actually put out information without a team's blessing. Love that for those people. And um yeah, I feel like the agent hasn't gotten enough criticism. He could have it was his job to avoid all this to protect Brandon, not to pretend to protect him. So feel bad for Brandon. I feel bad for the Niners. And I'm disgusted in that in that uh agent. Disgusted. And the the NFL PA, the NFL should have a rule about agents representing players and general managers, particularly ones on the same freaking team. It's disgusting. Anyway, that's all I have to say about that. Uh, to Brandon's credit, he hasn't posted anything since word got out that Kyle Shanahan was in a serious wreck. I doubt he knew. Trent Williams came out today and said he didn't know. I don't know if that's the truth, but I doubt Brandon knew. Um anyway, great day on the field for the 49ers. Great day for Brock and for Klay Kubak and for Kyle, but the AI situation tricky hasn't gone away yet. And this 11-day delay and the lack of information with the crash not going away yet. So everything on the field good for now, but the mark of a really good training camp is the focus is just what's on the field. And the Niners still have two things that are hanging over all this. One that they can't control, which is Kyle getting in a car accident. One they can't. That's the Brandon Iuk debacle. So to me, the smart move would be to move on from Brandon Iayuk, cut him, have that not be a topic anymore and then see see what silver linings may come out of Kyle Shanahan's hopefully hopefully short absence. And then Brandon, dude, Brandon, are you watching? Do you care? You need to hire a agent. Pardon my French. What are you doing, dude? You need to hire an agent. Otherwise, I'm just gonna assume you don't want to play football anymore. My heart goes out to you. Ryan Williams was a bad agent. You got screwed over. Go get another agent, please. I want to watch you play football, man. Come on. Anyway, I'm out. I got to go catch a train. Thanks for watching. No, he's not watching. Probably right. Take care. [music]

title: WR2 PLAN: Jayden Daniels, David Blough Give Commanders A Different Answer
text: Even without a solidified wide receiver two, Washington has what it needs to manufacture second receiver production. >> You are [music] Locked On Commanders, your daily podcast on the Washington Commanders, part of the Locked On Podcast Network, your team every day. >> Welcome inside today's episode of Locked On Commanders. I am your host, your guy on the ground, David Harrison, and today's episode is brought to you by Kalshi. For a limited time, download the Kalshi app, use the code locked on to get up to $500 in bonus credits when you trade just $25. And on today's episode, situational practice can rebuild Washington's close game edge, and Sonny Styles unlocks the linebacker trio if his coverage ability holds up. But first, how David Blough can create receiver two production through specialized roles. Hit the mailbag again as we progress our way towards NFL training camp, Washington Commanders training camp kicking off this Wednesday after or one Wednesday afternoon. Wednesday afternoon is when the episode will drop. Wednesday morning is when the practice will actually kick off. We had a question come through, can Jaden Daniels and David Blough make wide receiver two by committee an effective strategy this season? Mark came through the every dayer club mailbag, said, "I've listened all the episodes on the ceilings and floors, and yes, the quarterback is the most important. However, this year, especially the offensive coordinator is truly going to going to determine how far this team goes. Could this be a New England with Tom Brady type of offense where there's not too many big names on offense, but the system and quarterback make plays, everyone shines in given their own special talents. We've not seen what the running backs can do since we ran the ball out of shotgun, which doesn't keep the defense honest and doesn't give the running back the best opportunities to find lanes. If David Blough really challenges Jaden Daniels this year from under center, it can make Jaden Daniels excel, wide receiver two isn't a major concern. You just use a group of wide receivers as wide receiver two. What do you think? I think it's a great question. I think it's a great topic, and I think the question really is about whether or not a scheme can draw up a number two receiver when one doesn't presently offer itself up as an obvious choice. And I think yes, yes, as a matter of fact, it can because coaching absolutely matters. And to that end, David Blough, I don't think he's looking necessarily for a wide receiver two. He's looking for a second receiver. And if you're an everyday, you've been through these conversations. We've differentiated between the two. There is a difference between your wide receiver number two and your number two receiver. That's where this conversation kind of has to develop because when you look beyond just the receiver room and you see tight end Chigo Conkwo and running back Rashod White, you have two clear every down potential players who have receiver number two possibilities. And of course, you have De'Quan Cross Merritt who could develop that skill set. You have Ben Sinnott who hopefully is going to get more fully unlocked in this thing. You have Antonio Williams who is a rookie, so we don't know what he's going to be yet, but potentially could present that type of upside, right? Just last year, Chigo Conkwo came away with 56 catches, 560 yards, and two touchdowns for the Tennessee Titans, leading the Tennessee Titans in receiving. Meanwhile, Rashod White came away with 40 catches, 218 yards for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Chig alone would have walked away as the third leading receiver on the Commanders roster roster last year behind Zach Ertz and Deebo and third in receptions behind Deebo and Terry McLaurin. Uh third in receptions behind Ertz and Deebo, sorry. Third in receiving yards behind Deebo and Terry McLaurin. Rashod White also would have been third in receptions and would have been fifth in yards. Together, the two players combined, Chigo Conkwo and Rashod White, what they did last year, 96 catches, 778 yards, and two scores while playing for two non-playoff teams, both of which had their starting quarterbacks for all or most of the season, right? So, it's not what you should expect combined from these two players, but it is a good glimpse of what the two guys are available to do and potential or what potential they could bring to this offense given what David Blough is expected to do and given the talent level of Jayden Daniels. But we also use Ben Johnson as a barometer for what we might expect out of David Blau system. So, from 2022 to 2024, Ben Johnson was the OC for the Detroit Lions. Jared Goff was his quarterback. Jared Goff ranked among the quickest time to throw and among the shortest average depth of target. So, you're looking at a lot of quick throws, a lot of short targets. So, while Jayden has a nice deep ball, we know that Terry McLaurin can run and win deep routes with the best of them. This offense may be more predicated on presenting the threat of a deep shot while exploiting the room underneath that threat creates. And this doesn't mean that the deep ball is going to go away, it just means it's going to be more deliberate. When you look at Jared Goff, he regularly ranked middle of the pack when it came to deep ball attempts among starting quarterbacks while playing under offense coordinator Ben Johnson. But, he also had a 40-plus percentage completion rate on those deep ball attempts, putting him right at or inside the top 10. So, it was more quality than quantity. Whereas with Jayden Daniels, he was top 10 in deep ball attempts under Kliff Kingsbury, but he was bottom 10 in deep ball completion percentage, right? The main question now is how David Blau creates opportunities for role players because Philly, Dallas, Seattle, and Indianapolis are all probably going to be studying a good amount of Ben Johnson tape preparing for David Blau because, like us, they're going to kind of presume that a lot of this is going to be Ben Johnson-esque. Under center play action can make coverage more predictable. Jayden Daniels can spread those targets around to Antonio Williams, who we haven't seen yet, Chigo Okonkwo, the running backs, and then several other receivers. So, I think bottom line up front, David Blau can reduce how much Washington needs a conventional wide receiver two. But, he can't eliminate the need for secondary targets and for those targets to win. And he has them. They're not They may not be wide receiver number two, but he has receivers, players that can become available receivers, who are capable of being the second read on targets that are Terry McLaurin's first read, right? Would it be better or easier if David Blau had an established number two receiver like an Alec Pierce or a Romeo Dobbs or a Stefon Diggs or a healthy and focused Brandon Aiyuk? Yeah, it would absolutely be easier, right? But it doesn't mean it's impossible without one of those guys. They don't need that dominant number two wide receiver. They need a guy on the field every down who isn't Terry McLaurin who can still win outside, separate on third downs, threaten vertically, exploit linebackers and safeties and that Jahan Dotson can trust if his first read is not available. It's important to remember as well that a committee approach doesn't necessarily mean that every single player that could be that second receiver is going to get six targets. Doesn't mean that they're all just interchangeable players and doesn't mean that nobody has the chance of establishing themselves or that David Blough is going to rotate randomly until one of them just kind of sparks and becomes a superstar, right? What it should mean is that they're going to be specialized answers within this Washington Commanders offense. You know, David Blough also compared developing the pass-catching room like constructing a basketball roster where he doesn't want every single player to do the same type of thing. He also said the offense is being designed to put his best players in advantageous situations rather than requiring one fixed structure, which is really interesting because, you know, I've been asked some questions recently about like like Treylon Burks, right? Like where does Treylon Burks fit into this thing? And to be honest with you right now, the answer is kind of like I don't really know yet. You know, we have we have to kind of wait and see because from what we've seen from like a Ben Johnson type of offensive style and what we think that maybe David Blough is going to bring over from that Ben Johnson style, I don't know what he what he fits, right? Like we have some kind of clear like lid-lifting roles and things like that that we've talked about during this offseason and you see guys like Van Jefferson and Dyami Brown kind of fit those roles, but Van doesn't or Van Treylon doesn't really fit that role yet. Doesn't mean you know, there's not a role for him to fit into though and David Blough certainly could be working to figure out that role and and things like that, right? So, I think a bad committee, when you look at a committee approach, a bad committee is when you have several incomplete players who are being asked to do the exact same thing, right? And they just don't really fit. And then a good committee is kind of several different players who are being asked to do the jobs that they're best performed that they're best at performing.
